full_judgment:
While concurring with the main judgment just delivered by my learned brother Afzal, J in the case, I would like to add a few words of my own on some aspect of the chemical examination. 

 2. Facts of the case have been very ably set out and discussed by my learned brother and it is not necessary to go into those, section 510 of the Code of Criminal Procedure reads as follows:- 

 The report of the Chemical Examiner in the instant case was as follows:- 

 4. In the instant case, the post mortem examination was held on 11-8-67, the viscera and other parts of the body were sent from the Dacca Medical College Hospital to the Chemical Examiner on 30-10-67, the articles were received by the Chemical Examiner on 12-12-67, the report by the Chemical Examiner is dated 23-8-68 and it was received by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate on 10-10-68. There is no explanation why it took more than two months after the post mortem examination to send the articles from Dacca Medical College Hospital to the Chemical Examiner. Then again, there is no explanation why it took nearly two months for the articles from the date of dispatch to travel from Dacca Medical College Hospital to the Chemical Examiner at Mohakhali, Dacca. There is nothing on record to show how and through whom the articles were sent and in whose custody the articles were during this transit period. It is also not understood why it took nearly nine months for the Chemical Examiner to examine the articles and submit his report and then another two months to reach the Sub-Divisional Magistrate at Dacca from Mohakhali. The time gap between the post mortem examination and the receipt of the articles by the Chemical Examiner and the time taken between the receipt of the article by the Chemical Examiner and the submission of his report were so unduly long that it is likely to arouse suspicion in my reasonable mind, particularly in the absence of any explanation whatever either of the inordinate, delay or any evidence about the custody of those articles during the said period. In order to remove any suspicion it was not only the duty of the prosecution but it was essential for them to explain the inordinate delay between the post mortem examination and the report of the chemical examiner and to further show that during this long period of one year the articles were in safe custody without any chance of their being tampered with. But, the prosecution appears to be completely silent over this long unexplained period. 

 5. It is of the greatest importance in a case of poisoning that the substance found by the Chemical Examiner must be connected with or traced back to the articles removed or taken from the dead body of the person in the case. It well settled that if a fact is intended to be relied on by the prosecution, it must be proved with reasonable certainty and If such fact can only be established by proof of some subordinate facts, each of those subordinate facts must be proved with the same decree of the certainty as in required for the proof of the main fact. The omission to prove the necessary link may break the whole chain and thus deprive the prosecution of the opportunity of proving a valuable circumstantial evidences. 

 6. In the instant case I have noticed certain very significant or rather disquieting features. In the case of poisoning the onus clearly rests on the prosecution to prove that an article analyzed by the Chemical Examiner was actually the article sent to him for analysis in the case under trial in the same way as it is necessary for the prosecution to prove that a body sent for post-mortem examination was really the dead body of the person referred to in the case under trial. The Court must be satisfied that the connecting links necessary to prove the report of the postmortem examination or the chemical examination have been fully and duly established. It is true that the report of the Chemical Examiner is a piece of evidence that does not require any formal proof but it must be tendered in evidence and used as such to enable the accused to have an opportunity of assailing it, if he can. When the guilt or innocence of the accused rests solely on the opinion of the expert namely the Chemical Examiner, it is not only desirable but also in our opinion, necessary to examine the Chemical Examiner in Court to enable the accused to cross-examine the expert which was, of course done in the instant case. In the case of a murder by poison we do not think it is enough for the Chemical Examiner merely to say that except aconite or arsenic no other poison was detected. He must also state the grounds on which he arrives at that opinion. A perfunctory report as we had noticed in the instant case, may well lead to miscarriage of justice, more so when such opinion is held to be conclusive evidence on the point of guilt or innocence of the accused and where (he Court relies on such perfunctory report the case is actually decided by the Chemical Examiner and not by the Court. We feel that when a report is received from the Chemical Examiner it should be shown to the doctor who held the post-mortem examination to enable him to state what medico-legal inferences are to be drawn from such report. 

 7. Prosecution case, shortly stated, is that accused Monoruddin @ Mona held a Sunni feast at his house on the night of 23rd Sraban, 1373 B.S. corresponding to 9-8-67 on the occasion of his wife's alleged illness in which about 20/25 people including children participated. Deceased Maijuddin who was a member, probably of the union council, and a neighbor of accused Monoruddin, his house being only 2/21/2 pakkis away from that of the accused, was also invited there; but, at first, he did not go. At about 9 P.M. Monoruddin himself came and insisted upon the deceased to attend the feast whereupon the deceased being accompanied by one Mvi. Shahabuddin, a Zagir in this house, went to the house of the accused. There the deceased participated in the feast with others and at the end was served with a khili pan by accused Yaruddin Fakir which the accused Monoruddin had given even to him. All other invitees were served with pan on a plate but the deceased and Mvi. Shahabuddin were offered one khili each by accused Yaruddin Fakir. The dinner over, the deceased returned home and felt sick. He purged and vomited, complained of dryness of tongue, burning of the stomach and blurred vision. Then he fold his wife and other relations about serving of pan by accused Monoruddin and Yaruddin Fakir and before he could be given any medical attention, he died at about 3 A.M. 

 9. From the trend of cross-examination of P.Ws. it appears that the defense does not deny the prosecution case of taking food and, also pan by the deceased at the house of accused Monoruddin. What they deny is the alleged offering of special pan by the accused persons and their alleged administration of poison to the deceased through the said pan. It was suggested further that the wife of the deceased had illicit connection with Mvi. Shahabuddin and it might be that they had caused the death of the deceased. 

 10. Prosecution examined 18 witnesses in support or its case. The material aspect of the prosecution case, namely, the offering of the special pan by the accused persons to the deceased the taking of which made him sick and ultimately caused his death was sought to be proved by the direct evidence of those persons who were present at the feast. They include P. Ws. 3, 5, 6, 7 and 16. The other material part of the prosecution case that the deceased disclosed at his house immediately before his death that the accused persons had served him special pan and after taking it he felt ill was sought to be proved by P.Ws. 1, 2, 3, 5, and 9. It will be seem that amongst the aforesaid two groups P.Ws. 3 and 5 are common the former being the young son of the deceased and aged about 11/12 years and the other an invitee at the feast in the house of accused Monoruddin. We shall reproduce the evidence of P W 3 in details which will give a fair idea of the prosecution case and the kind of evidence upon which the prosecution relies. P.Ws. 13 and 14 are the Chemical Examiner and the doctor respectively. P.Ws.11 and 12 are the two boatmen who sought to prove that late in the night of occurrence accused Yaruddin Fakir asked them to take him to his village which they did not. P.W.15 is a constable and P.Ws.17 and 18 are the police officers who were connected with the investigation. 

 11. P.W. 3 Abdul Karim, young son of the deceased stated in his evidence that Helaluddin, son of accused Monoruddin came at about dusk and invited his father to their house in sinni function which was being held in connection with the illness of his mother; that he and his teacher Shahabuddin were also invited; that he went with Helal but his father and teacher did not go. He stated that accused Monoruddin came at 9 P. M. and persuaded his father who then went with Mvi. Shahabuddin and took meals along with others; that Monoruddin brought pan in a plate and gave two pans to Fakir taking out from inside the hut and Fakir gave those two pans- one to his father and another to Mvi. Shahabuddin which was seen by Shahjahan and Karam Ali. He also stated that on their way back home his father said that he was feeling sick, his tongue was burning and he was having burning sensation in his body. After reaching home he went to the latrine and after coming out from there complained of haziness of vision and burning of body and chest. The witness also stated that he then called Sanwar, Karam Ali and others to whom his father said that Mona gave pan to Fakir who then gave it to him and taking that pan he fell ill. The witness also stated that the uncle Habibur Rahman came at night and his father narrated the incident to him. His father died at 3 A. M. and before his death he said that Monoruddin had poisoned him. He further stated that 3/4 years back Monoruddin attempted to kill his father over which there was a case, but during the occurrences they were on good terms and used to take meal in each other's house. 

 12. As stated earlier, there are a number of P.Ws. who testified in support of the prosecution case as given out by P.W. 3. We shall take up the question of value and effect of the said oral evidence shortly. 

 13. Mr. Mostafa Kamal, the learned Advocate, appearing in support of the appeal, firstly, contended that the evidence of causing death by poisoning is not at all reliable and the conviction is based merely on suspicion. He has assailed the evidence of the Chemical Examiner as also his report Ext. 3 that the viscera contained aconite (poison) on various grounds and submitted that they are not worthy of belief and if that be so, the conviction cannot be sustained in law, the oral evidence notwithstanding. The learned Advocate has laid great emphasis on this part of the prosecution case and drawn our attention to the precise grounds taken in the memorandum of appeal. We may usefully reproduce some of those grounds which form the main part of his submissions. They are as follows:- 

 IX. For that the P.W. 13 the Chemical Examiner having stated in his examination-in-chief that on 12-12-1967 he received three parcels from Associate Professor of Medical Jurisprudence, Dacca Medical College in connection with Kaliakoir P.S.U.D. Case No. 9 dated 10-7-1967 consisting of two glass jars arid one glass phial which were sealed with impressions of a seal impression forwarded, and there being no evidence on record that the viscera of the deceased was forwarded to any Associate Professor of Medical Jurisprudence and no such Professor having been examined, and, further, there being no evidence on record that the viscera forwarded by P.W. 14 is the same examined by P.W. 13 earlier, prosecution has failed to identify the viscera of the deceased at all material stages and has furnished a disjointed, disrupted and incomplete history of the transmission of the viscera of the deceased from P.W. 14 to P.W. 13 and as such the Chemical Examiner is highly illegal and cannot be relied." 

 14. In a charge of murder by poisoning it is essential for the prosecution to prove, firstly, that the person alleged to have been murdered died of poisoning and second that the accused person or persons administered poison with intent to commit murder. Let us examine how far the prosecution has been able to prove in this case that deceased died of poisoning. The alleged poisoning was done at the house of accused Monoruddin through pan around 9/10 P. M. in the night of 9th August, 1977 and the deceased expired at about 3 A. M. the same night. Upon receiving the information of unnatural death from P.W. 4, an A.S.I. of Kaliakoir P.S. P.W. 17 came to the P. O. at 3-30 P. M. on 10-8-67 and forwarded the dead body to the Dacca Medical College Hospital for cross-examination through P.W. 15 constable Abdul Hakim. P.W. 14 Dr. Md. Fazlul Hoque held the postmortem examination. In his evidence he stated that in August 1967 he was posted at Green Road Staff Quarter Dispensary and on 11-8-67 he held post-mortem examination but found no visible wound on the person of the deceased. He stated that after dissecting the body he preserved the stomach, liver, lungs and heart for chemical examination. He also stated that the cause of death could not be ascertained but he suspected that it might be a case of poisoning and so the viscera was sent for chemical examination after preserving the same in sealed glass Jar. P.W. 13 the Chemical Examiner to the Government staled in his evidence that on 12-12-67 he received three parcels from the Associate Professor of Medical Jurisprudence, Dacca Medical College in connection with Kaliakoir PS UD/Case No 9 dated 10-8-67 consisting of two glass jars and one glass phial which was sealed with impression of a seal impression forwarded; one of the glass jars contained stomach with its contents, one glass jar contained portion of liver and one kidney and the glass phial contained spirit said to have been used as preservative. He stated that he detected aconite (poison) in viscera contained in the two glass jars but no poison in the contents of the glass phial. The seals were found correct and intact. He also stated that action of aconite is very quick in comparison to other poisons and it is prepared from some plant roots. In cross- examination he stated that he could not say as to how and from where the contents of jars were procured. 

 16. We have, however, found with profound dismay that the evidence with regard to the transmission of the viscera etc. of the deceased to the Chemical Examiner and the circumstances attending it are not at all clear and have provided ample room for doubting the identity of the matters sent for chemical examination. It is hardly necessary Jo mention that the report or for that matter the evidence of the Chemical Examiner is of little value unless there is clear proof of the identity of the matters examined by him. Prosecution must lead clear evidence to show the identity of the matters meant for chemical examination from its origin till they reach the Chemical Examiner so that there may not be any scope to doubt the identity of the matters at any stage. In the instant case we have no means of knowing as to who had the custody of the viscera etc. of the deceased from 11-8-67, the date of post-mortem examination, till it reached the Chemical Examiner on 12-12 67. Neither anybody from the Dacca Medical College Hospital nor from the police has, been examined to prove that the matters examined by the Chemical Examiner and those removed out of the body of the deceased by P.W.14 were one and the same. It appears that the viscera etc. were sent by the Associate Professor of Medical Jurisprudence Dacca Medical College by his Memo dated 30.10.67. We have failed to appreciate as to why it took about a month and a half to reach the chemical Examiner at Mohakhali, Dacca. No evidence has been led as to how or through whom it was sent. For these reasons, we are constrained to hold that the prosecution evidence in this behalf is rather disjointed and slip-shod which naturally leaves a gap, which again, needless to say, affects the whole prosecution case. We have also failed to appreciate as to why it took or should take more than 8 months for the Chemical Examiner to submit his report, This, we must say, is something very unusual and ought to have been explained. 

 18. In cases of poisoning by aconite the report and the evidence should be more detailed as it is found from the treaties that there are various species of aconite with varying capabilities.  20. Mr. Humayun Habibur Rasul, the learned Advocate, appearing for the state found it difficult to meet the criticisms that have been leveled against the report and the evidence of the Chemical Examiner and also as to absence of reliable evidence about the cause of death by poisoning, in view of our foregoing discussion we hold that the part of the prosecution case as to the death of the deceased by poisoning has not been satisfactorily established. 

 21. Mr. Mostafa Kamal has made elaborate submission on the oral evidence as well. He has pointed out the discrepancies and embellishments in. the evidence led by the prosecution. It will be sufficient if we take notice of the two broad things on facts as argued by the learned Advocate. He has submitted that conceding that the accused persons offered pan to the deceased after meal which ultimately caused his death, this fact alone is not altogether inconsistent with the innocence of the accused. The offering of a pan may at best cause suspicion as the man died soon thereafter but cannot be said to be conclusive evidence of a design to administer poison with intent to commit murder. Offering of a pan may as well be held to be a common Courtesy done to the respectable member who graciously took part in the sinni feast in the house of accused Monoruddin. Two circumstances have been pointed out in favour of the innocence of the accused persons which are inconsistent with the inference of guilt against them. Firstly, the P.Ws. (1 and 3) have stated that during the occurrence the deceased and accused Monoruddin were on good terms and they used to take meal in each others house. Secondly, P.Ws. 5, 7 and 8 have stated in their evidence that accused Monoruddin came to the house of the deceased after hearing about his illness in that night. We may also point out that the evidence on record goes to show that the deceased did not at all hesitate logo to the house of Monoruddin when the latter himself came to call him. Furthermore it cannot be ruled out altogether that the deceased might have got the poison just through accident by pan or otherwise and without the knowledge of his host. Thus we must say that the oral evidence cannot be held to be conclusive that the accused persons administered poison to the deceased through pan with intent to commit murder, specially because {here is no evidence of any motive at the time of the occurrence. Then Mr. Kamal pointed out that there is no mention about offering of pan by accused Yaruddin Fakir or about the disclosure by the deceased in his house before his death about offering of pan etc. by the accused persons in the FIR which was lodged by P.W.1 three weeks after the occurrence. We have noticed that the prosecution made a perceptible attempt to improve its case at the trial by ascribing some sort of a design to the accused person for murdering the deceased which was absent in the initial stage. When the occurrence took place, there was some suspicion against accused Monoruddin, which is only natural because of some previous enmity between him and the deceased. There was no mention about any role by accused Yaruddin Fakir in the matter of offering of pan to the deceased. This improvement is found only at the time of the trial. Be that as it may we do not think regard being bad to our findings above, that it is necessary to examine the evidence any further. We hold that in the facts and circumstances of the case the accused appellants are entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt. 

 22. In the result we allow this appeal, set aside the order of conviction and sentence, acquit the appellants and direct them to be set at liberty forthwith if not required in connection with any other case.
